topic.title: The counteroffer
topic.claim: Your counteroffer is the raise you were never offered: the day you resign, the budget appears.
topic.moment: Asking for a raise twice and hearing 'next cycle', then a meeting with a number two days after resigning.

turn.believed: the company suddenly values you more
turn.actually: the question changes from 'how does your raise compare with others' to 'what would replacing you cost'

topic.because: appraisal raises come from a fixed pool shared by everyone; a counteroffer is an off-cycle exception, approved because replacing someone costs more
topic.payoff: The real appraisal calendar has three dates: March, September, and the day you resign. Only one comes with a number.

cover.headline: The raise you were refused in April gets [approved the day you resign.]
cover.sub: Same company. Same you. A different question.

paragraphs: The raise you were refused in April gets approved the day you resign. Same company, same you. Something else changed.
slides.why_swipe: same company, same budget, so what changed?

paragraphs: April appraisal: "tough year, next cycle pakka." Your hike is a single digit, like everyone else in your band.
Then you resign on a Monday. By Wednesday there's a Teams invite called "Quick chat", and suddenly there's a number on the table.
slides.why_swipe: the scene is familiar; where did that number come from?

paragraphs: Here's what changed. In April, your raise was weighed against everyone else's.
The day you resign, the question in that room changes: what would it take to replace you? Months of hiring, a notice period, someone new learning your job.
**Next to that, your raise suddenly looks cheap.**
You feel flattered for about an hour. Then you do the maths on the last two years.
And if you take it, they now know your exit price. I've seen enough offices to know that number gets remembered next April.
slides.why_swipe: the honest downside is out; what was that meeting really about?

paragraphs: The number on the table was never really about your work.
**It was about the cost of the empty chair.**

end.save: Read it again before your next appraisal conversation.
end.send: Send it to the colleague who's heard "next cycle pakka" twice.

draft.caption: Has a resignation ever got you the raise your appraisal didn't?

sources.quote: Employees with a compa-ratio below 100% might receive large, merit-based raises to keep their pay competitive, whereas highly experienced employees who are already paid above market value may be rewarded for excellence in smaller increments.
This two-variable merit matrix combines performance metrics with compa ratio, which compares an employee's salary to the midpoint of their salary band.

The pool sets how much money there is; the performance rating and compa-ratio then combine in a merit matrix that turns those inputs into a number for each person. A bigger increase for one person means a smaller one for someone else.
For employers, retention is at a premium as they seek to avoid the replacement costs of recruiting and retraining new employees.
it costs a business approximately $4,000 and 3 months to hire, recruit and onboard a new employee
When the company ignores internal pay fairness, a public counteroffer may place the resigning employee close to, or even above, colleagues with greater experience.

ledger.text: During regular appraisal cycles, an employee's raise is decided by comparison with peers in the same band, not on individual merit alone.
ledger.sentence: In April, your raise was weighed against everyone else's.

ledger.text: When an employee resigns, companies evaluate a counteroffer based on the cost of replacing that person (hiring time, notice period, time for a replacement to learn the job) rather than peer comparison.
ledger.sentence: The day you resign, the question in that room changes: what would it take to replace you? Months of hiring, a notice period, someone new learning your job.

ledger.text: Because the cost of replacing an employee is higher than the cost of a raise, companies approve on resignation the same raise they refused during appraisal.
ledger.sentence: Next to that, your raise suddenly looks cheap.

ledger.text: Once an employee accepts a counteroffer, the employer notes the compensation figure it took to retain them and factors it into the employee's next appraisal cycle.
ledger.sentence: I've seen enough offices to know that number gets remembered next April.

mechanism.broken_premise: None fail. Premise 4 is the weakest — the specific 'your exit price gets remembered as a number and used against you next April' is more folk wisdom than a documented line-item mechanism — but it is directionally supported: accepting a counteroffer measurably marks the employee's standing, so the take does not break on it.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Appraisal raises come from a fixed merit pool (median ~3.7% of payroll) that a merit matrix splits across peers by performance rating and position in the salary band (compa-ratio), so your raise is literally rationed against everyone else's. A resignation moves the decision to a different budget and a different question — retention/out-of-cycle spend judged against replacement cost (recruiting, notice period, lost productivity, ramp-up), which runs from ~20% of salary for ordinary roles to 50–200% for skilled and senior ones — which is why a raise that looked unaffordable in April looks cheap on Wednesday. Accepting then flags you: a large share of employers treat counteroffer-takers as flight risks with diminished standing, which feeds into promotion, review and layoff decisions, so the retention number genuinely follows you.

sources.quote: For all positions except executives and physicians... the typical (median) cost of turnover was 21 percent of an employee's annual salary.
SHRM estimates that replacing an employee costs between 50% and 200% of their annual salary once hiring, onboarding, and the productivity gap are accounted for.

A merit matrix maps an employee's performance rating against their compa-ratio... so someone paid below the midpoint gets a higher increase than a peer at the top of the band with the same rating — the raise is allocated from a fixed, finance-set budget across the group.
78% of employers view employees who accepted counteroffers as passive job seekers going forward, and this perception affects everything from your next performance review to layoff decisions.
